1058.title: Rohatsu
1058.hook: the week of sitting before December 8
1058.howItsDone: In Japanese Zen, monasteries and practice groups keep Rohatsu as a week of intensive sitting that ends on the day observed as the Buddha's awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kathina a third time: a robe sewn like rice fields and used until the last shreds went into the plaster. Your line: the robe given. What did you give? Day one thousand fifty-eight.

What shows up when you sit still for a long time? Not two minutes. Days. In Japanese Zen, the week that ends on the day kept for the Buddha's awakening is called Rohatsu, and it is a week of sitting, from before dawn into the night. Last year you met the end of that week: the last night and the morning star. This year, stay in the middle of it, the long hours when the mind brings out everything it has. An old poem has a name for all of it.
screen: `WHAT SHOWS UP IN A LONG SIT?` → `A WEEK OF SITTING.` → `AN OLD POEM NAMES IT.`

segments.voice: The poem is in the Sutta Nipata, and it's called the Padhana Sutta, the discourse on striving. The young seeker is by a river, worn thin from effort, and Mara comes to him. Mara doesn't arrive with weapons. He arrives kindly. You're thin, he says. You're close to death. Live. Live, and do good deeds. Why wear yourself out like this? It's a reasonable voice. That's the trouble with it. And the seeker answers by naming Mara's army, one troop at a time. Desires. Discontent. Hunger and thirst. Craving. Sloth and drowsiness. Fear. Doubt. Hypocrisy and stubbornness. And then gain, fame and honor, and praising yourself while looking down on others. Listen to that list again. There isn't a monster in it. It's the inside of a long sit. Aching legs, and the voice that says this is pointless. Hunger an hour before lunch. Sleep pulling at the eyelids after midday. Doubt asking who you think you are. A little pride, too, about how well you're sitting. The poem's weapon isn't force. The seeker says he will break this army with wisdom, the way a stone breaks an unbaked clay pot: see each troop clearly, name it, and not get up. In the poem's own picture, he would rather fall in battle than live on defeated. And at the end, Mara gives up. His lute slips from under his arm, and he disappears. So a week of Rohatsu isn't only endurance. It's the same scene played again, in a cold hall, by ordinary people, with the troops arriving on schedule and being named as they come.
screen: `MARA ARRIVES KINDLY.` · `THE SEEKER NAMES THE ARMY.` · `IT'S THE INSIDE OF A LONG SIT.` · then, large: `SEE IT, NAME IT, DON'T GET UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. The bell will hold two minutes. Sit, and as each thing turns up, name it quietly with the poem's words: desire, discontent, hunger, sleepiness, fear, doubt. Name it, and stay where you are. You don't have to win. You only have to notice and not get up. Later today, if you have the time, sit ten minutes more than you planned, and see which of the army comes to visit. The bell holds the time.
Rohatsu. The Zen week of sitting that ends on the day kept for the Buddha's awakening, when the old army comes and gets named. Today's word.
Your line: the week of sitting. Today, when one of Mara's troops turns up, boredom, a craving, a doubt, call it by name and stay one more minute. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

1059.title: The day of miracles
1059.hook: Chotrul Duchen, the Tibetan festival at the end of Losar's first fortnight
1059.howItsDone: On Chotrul Duchen, Tibetan Buddhists visit temples, light butter lamps, give to monks and to people in need, and make offerings, holding that deeds done on this day are multiplied.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rohatsu: Mara's army named troop by troop, desire, sleepiness, doubt, and the seeker who didn't get up. Your line: the week of sitting. Which troop came to visit? Day one thousand fifty-nine.

In the city of Rajagaha, a sandalwood bowl hangs at the top of a tall pole, high above the street. A rich merchant has put it there as a test: let any holy man with real powers rise up and take it. Teachers of other schools come and ask for the bowl, but none of them rises. Then a monk named Pindola lifts into the air, takes the bowl, and comes down to a cheering crowd. It sounds like a triumph. The Buddha did not see it that way. Today, miracles, and a Tibetan festival named for them.
screen: `A BOWL ON A TALL POLE.` → `PINDOLA RISES AND TAKES IT.` → `THE BUDDHA ISN'T PLEASED.`

segments.voice: In the Vinaya, the Buddha rebukes Pindola: all that, for the sake of a wooden bowl, to impress a crowd. He has the bowl broken into pieces and given to the monks to grind for ointment, and he makes a rule. Monks are not to display superhuman powers to lay people. The tradition then tells a second story, in the commentary on the Dhammapada. Rival teachers hear about the rule and decide the Buddha can no longer perform a wonder, so they challenge him. He answers that the rule binds his disciples, not himself, the way a king's rule about his orchard binds everyone but the king. And at Savatthi, tradition says, he performs the twin miracle: fire and water streaming from his body at once. Tibetan Buddhists remember the Buddha's wonders at Chotrul Duchen, the day of miracles, which comes at the full moon closing the first fortnight of the new year. Tradition says that on this day the results of what you do, good or harmful, are multiplied many times. So people light butter lamps, give, and make offerings. In the Kevaddha Sutta, the Buddha sorts wonders into kinds. He names three: the wonder of power, the wonder of reading minds, and the wonder of instruction. The first two, he says, can look like a charm or a trick, and he turns away from them. The one he praises is instruction, teaching that changes how someone lives. And a verse in the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, points to a quieter kind of wonder: "If a man does what is good, let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good." Set beside the festival, that verse gives the multiplying a plain shape: do the good thing a second time.
screen: `THE BOWL GROUND TO POWDER.` · `THE TWIN MIRACLE AT SAVATTHI.` · `THREE WONDERS, ONE PRAISED.` · then, large: `LET HIM DO IT AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: do one kind thing twice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one kind thing you did recently. Small is fine: a message sent, a door held, a meal shared. Let yourself enjoy remembering it, the way the verse says, delight in it. Then, without hurrying, choose how you'll do it again today, for the same person or someone new. See yourself doing it. The bell holds the time.
The day of miracles. Chotrul Duchen, when Tibetan Buddhists remember the Buddha's wonders and, tradition says, every deed counts many times over. Today's word.
Your line: good deeds multiply. Today, do one kind thing, then do it again before the day is out, and enjoy it both times. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

screen: `DAY 1059 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE YEAR IN ONE SITTING.`

1060.title: The year in one sitting
1060.hook: the poem, the disciples, the songs, the tales, the roads, the teachers, the history
1060.tomorrow: Year three close: the great story
1060.howItsDone: Some Buddhist communities mark the end of a period of study or a retreat with a longer sitting and a review of what was learned, sometimes followed by a dedication of merit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the day of miracles: Pindola's bowl ground to powder, the twin miracle, and a verse that says do the good thing again. Your line: good deeds multiply. Did you do it twice? Day one thousand sixty.

Near the top of a long climb, a hiker stops, turns around, and looks back down the trail. From up there the switchbacks that felt endless are just a few lines on a hillside, and the whole path makes sense at once. Tomorrow this year closes. So today, before the last step, turn around. One sitting, one look back over a year that began with a poem and ended with festivals.
screen: `STOP NEAR THE TOP.` → `TURN AROUND.` → `ONE LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: It began with a poem. Ashvaghosha's Buddhacarita told the life as an epic: the palace, the king's fear, and the old man the gods placed on the prince's road so that he would see. Then came the disciples. Sariputta and Moggallana, the friends who went looking together. Ananda, who remembered. Mahakassapa in his rag robe. The women who asked to be ordained, and the whole sangha, wise and proud and forgetful, all welcome. Then the songs of the elders, in their own words: Patacara watching a lamp's wick drawn down until the flame went out, and Mutta, free of the mortar, the pestle and her crooked husband. Then the long tales of the Jataka: Sumedha lying down in the mud so a Buddha of the past could walk across him, and the caravan leader who kept the water when spirits told him to throw it away. Then the roads. Councils where the elders recited the teaching from memory. Monks traveling with merchants along the Silk Road, translators like Kumarajiva, and Faxian setting out on foot for India. Then the teachers: Nagarjuna's middle way, Asanga tending a wounded dog, Shantideva, thought lazy, standing up to recite a long poem on the bodhisattva's way. Then history, held honestly: monasteries closed and reopened, Cambodia's sangha rebuilt from few, the empty niches at Bamiyan. And these last days, the festival year: a lamp at Vesak, sweet tea for the baby Buddha, a circle dance, a robe, a week of sitting, a day of miracles. Look at it from up here. The switchbacks were a poem, a song, a tale, a road, a teacher, a hard chapter. From this height they are one trail, and you walked all of it.
screen: `A POEM, THEN THE DISCIPLES.` · `SONGS AND LONG TALES.` · `ROADS, TEACHERS, HISTORY.` · then, large: `ONE TRAIL, SEEN FROM ABOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. The bell will hold two minutes now. The path suggests twenty, so if you have them later today, give the year twenty minutes. For now, sit, and let one picture from this year come back by itself. Don't choose it. Whatever arrives first: a lamp, a bowl, a road, a dog, a robe, a face. Stay with it. Notice what your mind kept when you weren't trying to keep anything. The bell holds the time.
The year in one sitting. Year three, seen whole: the poem, the disciples, the songs, the tales, the roads, the teachers, the history, the festivals. Today's word.
screen: `THE YEAR IN ONE SITTING — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: look how far. Today, tell someone one story from this year, the one that stayed with you, in two sentences. Day one thousand sixty.

screen: `DAY 1060 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR THREE CLOSE: THE GREAT STORY.`

1061.title: Year three close: the great story
1061.hook: the whole story from the palace to today
1061.howItsDone: Buddhists tell the Buddha's life and the story of the teaching at festivals, in temple paintings and in chanting, and some communities close a year of study by dedicating its merit to others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole year in one sitting: the poem, the disciples, the songs, the tales, the roads, the teachers, the history. Your line: look how far. Which story did you tell? Day one thousand sixty-one.

A gate opens in the middle of the night, and a prince rides out of his father's palace. In the poem that opened this year, that night is the turning point of the great story. It doesn't end there, and it doesn't end with him. It runs on, hand to hand, road to road, until it reaches a temple down some street near you, a lamp lit on a windowsill, a person sitting still for two minutes on an ordinary morning. Today, the last day of year three, the whole story in one telling, from that gate to today.
screen: `A GATE OPENS AT NIGHT.` → `HAND TO HAND, ROAD TO ROAD.` → `FROM THE GATE TO TODAY.`

segments.voice: The prince sees age, sickness and death, and a wanderer at peace, and he leaves. He strives until he is thin as a shadow. He sits beneath a tree, and Mara comes with his army of desire and doubt, and the seeker doesn't get up. He wakes up. He walks to the deer park and turns the wheel of the teaching for his old companions. Friends come, then strangers, then kings and courtesans and outcasts. Women ask to be ordained, and an order of nuns begins. For years he walks the roads and teaches, and at the end, lying between two trees, he gives his last instruction, the one you heard on the day of renewal: in paraphrase, all made things come apart, so keep going with care. Then the story passes to other hands. The elders meet and recite what they remember. Reciters carry it by memory; later, tradition says, scribes write it down. An emperor carves teachings into stone. Monks and nuns carry it south across the sea, and north along the caravan roads, into new languages. Teachers argue and explain and build new schools on it. Buddhists tell some parts differently: which texts come first, which teachers matter most. Each school keeps its own telling. Then the hard chapters: monasteries burned, monks killed, texts lost. And each time someone gathers what's left and begins again. Which brings the story here, to temples far from where it started, to chaplains in hospitals, to festivals with sweet tea and lamps. A story that started with one person leaving home is now kept by people in many homes.
screen: `THE PALACE, THE TREE, THE DEER PARK.` · `KEEP GOING WITH CARE.` · `MEMORY, STONE, ROADS AND SCHOOLS.` · then, large: `BROKEN, AND BEGUN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: rest, and look out. If there's a window near you, turn toward it. If not, a doorway, or just the far side of the room. Sit, and let your eyes rest on what's out there without naming it. The story you heard this year went out through a palace gate and onto the roads. Let your attention go out the same way, gently, as far as it likes, and then come back to the breath. Nothing to finish. Just rest. The bell holds the time.
Year three close. The great story, from the palace gate to the people keeping it today, and the end of the third year on this path. Today's word.
Your line: you know the story now. Today, look out a window for one quiet minute before the next thing. Tomorrow, year four opens with the higher teaching. Day one thousand sixty-one.
